prompt: If a change in conditions raises the energy of the reactants but leaves the transition-state energy unchanged, what happens to ΔG‡ and the reaction rate?

choices.text: ΔG‡ decreases and the reaction gets faster
ΔG‡ increases and the reaction gets slower
choices.why: That's the effect of lowering the reactant energy or raising the transition-state energy.

choices.text: ΔG‡ decreases but the reaction gets slower
choices.why: A smaller ΔG‡ means a faster reaction, not a slower one.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because only the transition-state energy matters
choices.why: ΔG‡ is the energy difference between the reactant ground state and the transition state, so the reactant level matters too.

explanation: The rate is set by ΔG‡, the energy difference between reactant ground state and transition state. Raising the reactant energy or lowering the transition-state energy decreases ΔG‡ and increases the rate; lowering the reactant energy or raising the transition-state energy does the reverse.

prompt: According to the section's summary, how does steric hindrance in the substrate slow an S_N2 reaction?

choices.text: It raises the energy of the transition state, increasing ΔG‡
It lowers the energy of the transition state, decreasing ΔG‡
choices.why: A smaller ΔG‡ would mean a faster reaction. Hindrance makes the transition state harder to reach.

choices.text: It lowers the ground-state energy of the nucleophile, increasing ΔG‡
choices.why: That's how protic solvents slow S_N2 reactions. Substrate effects are felt mainly in the transition state.

choices.text: It makes the leaving group a stronger base, so it departs less easily
choices.why: Steric hindrance concerns the groups crowding the reacting carbon, not the basicity of the leaving group.

explanation: A hindered carbon is shielded from the incoming nucleophile, so the transition state, with its partial Nu–C bond, is higher in energy. That increases ΔG‡ and decreases the rate. As a result, S_N2 reactions are best for methyl and primary substrates.

prompt: Which list ranks these bromides from most to least reactive in the S_N2 reaction: CH3CH2CH2Br, (CH3)3CCH2Br, (CH3)2CHBr, CH3Br?

choices.text: CH3Br > CH3CH2CH2Br > (CH3)2CHBr > (CH3)3CCH2Br
CH3Br > (CH3)3CCH2Br > CH3CH2CH2Br > (CH3)2CHBr
choices.why: (CH3)3CCH2Br is primary, but as a neopentyl halide its branching one carbon away greatly hinders S_N2, putting it below the secondary bromide.

choices.text: (CH3)3CCH2Br > (CH3)2CHBr > CH3CH2CH2Br > CH3Br
choices.why: That is the reverse. Methyl halides are by far the most reactive substrates in S_N2 reactions.

choices.text: CH3CH2CH2Br > CH3Br > (CH3)2CHBr > (CH3)3CCH2Br
choices.why: Methyl halides are more reactive than primary ones, because the methyl carbon is the least hindered.

explanation: The section's S_N2 reactivity order is methyl > primary > secondary > neopentyl > tertiary. So CH3Br (methyl) > CH3CH2CH2Br (primary) > (CH3)2CHBr (secondary) > (CH3)3CCH2Br (neopentyl).

prompt: What effect does the branching in a tert-butyl halide (a tertiary halide) have on the S_N2 reaction?

choices.text: It effectively halts the reaction
It slows the reaction only slightly
choices.why: Even the branching in an isopropyl (secondary) halide slows the reaction greatly; tertiary branching effectively stops it.

choices.text: It speeds the reaction up
choices.why: More substituents on the reacting carbon mean more steric hindrance, which slows S_N2 reactions.

choices.text: It has no effect on the rate
choices.why: Substrate structure is a major S_N2 variable: a crowded carbon is shielded from the nucleophile.

explanation: Alkyl branching at the reacting center, as in isopropyl halides (2°), slows the S_N2 reaction greatly, and further branching, as in tert-butyl halides (3°), effectively halts it. Tertiary substrates do not react by an S_N2 mechanism.

prompt: 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, (CH3)3CCH2Br, is a primary halide, yet it reacts very slowly by S_N2. Why?

choices.text: Branching one carbon away from the reacting center still hinders the nucleophile
It is really a tertiary halide, because it contains a tert-butyl group
choices.why: The bromine-bearing carbon is bonded to only one other carbon, so it's primary. The branching sits one carbon away.

choices.text: Bromide ion is a poor leaving group, so the C–Br bond doesn't break
choices.why: Bromide is a good leaving group, a weak base. The problem is steric.

choices.text: It reacts by way of a carbocation, which the bulky group destabilizes
choices.why: The S_N2 reaction has no carbocation intermediate. The slowness comes from hindered backside approach.

explanation: Even branching one carbon away from the reacting center, as in 2,2-dimethylpropyl (neopentyl) halides, greatly hinders nucleophilic displacement. In the section's order, neopentyl halides are less reactive than secondary ones.

prompt: Why are vinylic halides (R2C=CRX) and aryl halides unreactive toward S_N2 displacement?

choices.text: Backside attack would have to come in the plane of the double bond, through part of the molecule
Their halide ions are strong bases, so they are too poor as leaving groups to be displaced
choices.why: Halide ions are weak bases and good leaving groups. The problem is the blocked path for backside attack.

choices.text: They react so fast by S_N2 that the reaction can't be followed or measured
choices.why: They are unreactive toward S_N2 displacement, not too fast to measure.

choices.text: Their carbon–halogen bonds lie in a plane that the nucleophile can approach from either side
choices.why: If backside approach were easy, they would react. The trouble is that the backside path runs through the molecule itself.

explanation: The lack of reactivity of vinylic and aryl halides is due to steric factors: the incoming nucleophile would have to approach in the plane of the carbon–carbon double bond and burrow through part of the molecule to carry out a backside displacement.

prompt: What does a species need in order to act as a nucleophile in an S_N2 reaction?

choices.text: An unshared pair of electrons, making it a Lewis base
A full negative charge on the reacting atom
choices.why: Neutral species such as H2O and NH3 are nucleophiles too. What's needed is an unshared electron pair.

choices.text: An empty orbital, making it a Lewis acid
choices.why: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. A nucleophile donates one to carbon.

choices.text: A hydrogen atom that it can give up as a proton
choices.why: Nucleophiles such as I− and Cl− have no hydrogen at all. The requirement is an unshared electron pair.

explanation: Any species, either neutral or negatively charged, can act as a nucleophile as long as it has an unshared pair of electrons, that is, as long as it is a Lewis base. A negatively charged nucleophile gives a neutral product; a neutral nucleophile gives a positively charged product.

prompt: According to Table 11.3.1, how many times faster does hydroxide ion (HO−) react with bromomethane than water does?
explanation: Table 11.3.1 gives relative rates of 1 for H2O and 10,000 for HO−, so hydroxide reacts 10,000 times faster. Negatively charged nucleophiles are usually more reactive than neutral ones.

prompt: In Table 11.3.1, the relative rate of reaction with bromomethane is 100,000 for iodide ion and 1,000 for chloride ion. How many times faster does iodide react?
explanation: 100,000 ÷ 1,000 = 100. This fits the trend that nucleophilicity usually increases going down a column of the periodic table: I− > Br− > Cl−.

prompt: In Table 11.3.1, the relative rate of reaction with bromomethane is 125,000 for cyanide ion and 10,000 for hydroxide ion. How many times faster does cyanide react?
explanation: 125,000 ÷ 10,000 = 12.5. Cyanide gives acetonitrile, CH3CN, and is tied with hydrosulfide (HS−) as the fastest nucleophile in the table.

prompt: According to Table 11.3.1, what product forms when ammonia, NH3, reacts with bromomethane?

choices.text: CH3NH3+, methylammonium ion
CH3NH2, a neutral amine
choices.why: A neutral nucleophile gives a positively charged product. The table lists methylammonium ion, CH3NH3+.

choices.text: CH3OH2+, methylhydronium ion
choices.why: That is the product with water, the slowest nucleophile in the table.

choices.text: CH3CN, acetonitrile
choices.why: That is the product with cyanide ion.

explanation: Ammonia is a neutral nucleophile, so its substitution product is positively charged: NH3 + CH3Br → CH3NH3+ (methylammonium ion) + Br−. Its relative rate is 700.

prompt: According to Table 11.3.1, which of these nucleophiles reacts fastest with bromomethane?

choices.text: HS−
HO−
choices.why: Hydroxide's relative rate is 10,000, well below hydrosulfide's 125,000.

choices.text: Cl−
choices.why: Chloride's relative rate is only 1,000.

choices.text: CH3CO2−
choices.why: Acetate's relative rate is only 500.

explanation: Hydrosulfide ion (HS−) has a relative rate of 125,000 (tied with cyanide), compared with 10,000 for HO−, 1,000 for Cl− and 500 for CH3CO2−. HS− being more nucleophilic than HO− reflects the increase in nucleophilicity going down a column.

prompt: HO− is both more basic and more nucleophilic than acetate ion, CH3CO2−, which in turn is more basic and more nucleophilic than H2O. Which trend does this illustrate?

choices.text: Nucleophilicity roughly parallels basicity for nucleophiles with the same reacting atom
Nucleophilicity increases going down a column of the periodic table
choices.why: That trend compares different reacting atoms, such as S and O. All three of these react through oxygen.

choices.text: Nucleophilicity decreases as basicity increases
choices.why: It's the opposite here: the more basic species is also the more nucleophilic.

choices.text: Neutral nucleophiles are more reactive than charged ones
choices.why: Negatively charged nucleophiles are usually more reactive. Neutral H2O is the slowest of the three.

explanation: Nucleophilicity roughly parallels basicity when comparing nucleophiles that have the same reacting atom. Nucleophilicity is the affinity of a Lewis base for carbon and basicity is its affinity for a proton, so the two tend to go together.

prompt: Which is the more reactive nucleophile, H2O or H2S, and why?

choices.text: H2S, because nucleophilicity usually increases going down a column of the periodic table
H2O, because oxygen holds its valence electrons more tightly than sulfur does
choices.why: Tightly held electrons are less reactive. Sulfur's valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more reactive.

choices.text: H2O, because nucleophilicity always parallels basicity
choices.why: That trend applies to nucleophiles with the same reacting atom. Here the reacting atoms are different, O and S.

choices.text: Neither, because both are neutral and react at the same rate
choices.why: Charge isn't the only factor. Going down a column, nucleophilicity usually increases.

explanation: Going down the periodic table, elements have their valence electrons in successively larger shells, farther from the nucleus, less tightly held and more reactive. So H2S is more nucleophilic than H2O (Exercise 11.3.2), just as HS− is more nucleophilic than HO−.

prompt: Which is the more reactive nucleophile, (CH3)3N or (CH3)3B?

choices.text: (CH3)3N, because nitrogen has an unshared pair of electrons
(CH3)3B, because boron has an empty orbital
choices.why: An empty orbital makes boron an electron-pair acceptor, a Lewis acid, not a nucleophile.

choices.text: Neither, because both are neutral and react equally
choices.why: (CH3)3B has no unshared electron pair, so it can't act as a nucleophile at all.

choices.text: (CH3)3B, because boron is less electronegative than nitrogen
choices.why: Without an unshared electron pair, boron has nothing to donate to carbon.

explanation: A nucleophile must have an unshared pair of electrons (be a Lewis base). Nitrogen in (CH3)3N has a lone pair; boron in (CH3)3B has none, so (CH3)3N is the nucleophile (Exercise 11.3.2).

prompt: Which is the more reactive nucleophile, (CH3)2N− or (CH3)2NH?

choices.text: (CH3)2N−, because negatively charged nucleophiles are usually more reactive
(CH3)2NH, because its N–H bond makes it more nucleophilic
choices.why: An N–H bond doesn't add nucleophilicity. The negatively charged anion is the more reactive one.

choices.text: (CH3)2NH, because neutral nucleophiles give neutral products
choices.why: Neutral nucleophiles give positively charged products, and they're usually less reactive than anions.

choices.text: Neither, because both react through the same nitrogen atom
choices.why: With the same reacting atom, nucleophilicity parallels basicity, and the anion is the stronger base.

explanation: Negatively charged nucleophiles are usually more reactive than neutral ones, so (CH3)2N− beats (CH3)2NH (Exercise 11.3.2). For the same reason, S_N2 reactions are often carried out under basic conditions rather than neutral or acidic ones.

prompt: What product forms from the S_N2 reaction of 1-bromobutane with lithium acetylide, H–C≡C–Li?

choices.text: 1-hexyne
1-butyne
choices.why: The acetylide carbon bonds to the butyl group, so the product has 4 + 2 = 6 carbons, not 4.

choices.text: 1-pentyne
choices.why: The butyl group has 4 carbons and the acetylide 2, giving 6 carbons, not 5.

choices.text: 2-hexyne
choices.why: The new C–C bond forms at the end of the butyl chain, leaving the triple bond at the chain end: HC≡CCH2CH2CH2CH3.

explanation: The acetylide anion displaces bromide in an S_N2 reaction (as in Section 9.8): HC≡C− + CH3CH2CH2CH2Br → HC≡CCH2CH2CH2CH3 (1-hexyne) + Br− (Exercise 11.3.1).

prompt: What product forms from the S_N2 reaction of 1-bromobutane with ammonia, NH3?

choices.text: Butylammonium bromide
1-butanol
choices.why: 1-Butanol forms with KOH (hydroxide nucleophile). Ammonia is a nitrogen nucleophile.

choices.text: 1-iodobutane
choices.why: 1-Iodobutane forms with NaI (iodide nucleophile).

choices.text: Methylammonium bromide
choices.why: Methylammonium ion comes from ammonia and bromomethane. With 1-bromobutane, a butyl group ends up on nitrogen.

explanation: Ammonia is a neutral nucleophile, so the S_N2 product is positively charged: CH3CH2CH2CH2NH3+ with Br− as its counterion, butylammonium bromide (Exercise 11.3.1).

prompt: Which list ranks these leaving groups from most reactive to least reactive in S_N2 reactions?

choices.text: TosO− > I− > Br− > Cl− > F−
F− > Cl− > Br− > I− > TosO−
choices.why: That's reversed. Fluoride is a poor leaving group, and tosylate is the best of these.

choices.text: I− > TosO− > Br− > Cl− > F−
choices.why: Tosylates are even more reactive than halides in nucleophilic substitutions.

choices.text: TosO− > F− > Cl− > Br− > I−
choices.why: Among the halides the order is I− > Br− > Cl− > F−. Fluoride isn't displaced by nucleophiles.

explanation: The best leaving groups best stabilize the negative charge in the transition state, so they are the weakest bases. The section's order rises from F− through Cl− and Br− to I− and then TosO−, with HO−, H2N− and RO− so poor that they aren't displaced.

prompt: Which of these classes of compounds does not typically undergo S_N2 reactions?

choices.text: Alkyl fluorides
Alkyl iodides
choices.why: Iodide is a good leaving group, a weak base, so alkyl iodides react readily.

choices.text: Alkyl tosylates
choices.why: Tosylates are even more reactive than halides in nucleophilic substitutions.

choices.text: Alkyl bromides
choices.why: Bromide is a good leaving group, a weak base, so alkyl bromides react readily.

explanation: F−, HO−, RO− and H2N− are not displaced by nucleophiles. In other words, alkyl fluorides, alcohols, ethers and amines do not typically undergo S_N2 reactions.

prompt: Why are weak bases such as Cl−, Br− and tosylate ion good leaving groups in S_N2 reactions?

choices.text: They stabilize the negative charge in the transition state well, lowering its energy
They raise the ground-state energy of the nucleophile
choices.why: That's what polar aprotic solvents do. Leaving-group effects are felt mainly in the transition state.

choices.text: They are the strongest nucleophiles available
choices.why: Leaving ability depends on stabilizing the departing negative charge, not on attacking carbon.

choices.text: They are strong bases that pull the bonding electrons away from carbon
choices.why: Cl−, Br− and tosylate are weak bases. Strong bases such as OH− and NH2− make poor leaving groups.

explanation: The leaving group is usually expelled with a negative charge, so the best leaving groups are those that best stabilize negative charge in the transition state. The greater the stabilization, the lower the transition-state energy and the faster the reaction. Groups that best stabilize a negative charge are the weakest bases.

prompt: An alcohol can be made reactive toward S_N2 substitution by converting it into a tosylate with para-toluenesulfonyl chloride. What happens to the configuration of the oxygen-bearing carbon in this step?

choices.text: It stays the same, because the C–O bond is not broken
It is inverted, because the tosyl group attacks the carbon from the back side
choices.why: Tosylate formation doesn't break the C–O bond, so nothing happens at the carbon itself.

choices.text: It is racemized, because a carbocation forms on the way to the tosylate
choices.why: No carbocation forms; the C–O bond stays intact throughout.

choices.text: The carbon becomes planar and achiral in the tosylate product
choices.why: The carbon keeps its four bonds and its configuration. Only the O–H hydrogen is replaced.

explanation: Tosylate formation does not change the configuration of the oxygen-bearing carbon because the C–O bond is not broken. The tosylate is then even more reactive than a halide in nucleophilic substitution.

prompt: Propene oxide reacts with HCl by an S_N2 backside attack. What is the product?

choices.text: 1-chloro-2-propanol, from attack at the less hindered primary carbon
2-chloro-1-propanol, from attack at the more hindered secondary carbon
choices.why: The S_N2 backside attack takes place at the less hindered primary carbon.

choices.text: 1,2-propanediol, from attack by water
choices.why: With HCl the nucleophile is chloride. 1,2-Diols form when epoxides react with aqueous acid.

choices.text: No product, because ethers don't undergo S_N2 reactions
choices.why: Epoxides are the exception: angle strain in the three-membered ring makes them much more reactive than other ethers.

explanation: Because of the angle strain in their three-membered ring, epoxides are much more reactive than other ethers. Propene oxide reacts with HCl to give 1-chloro-2-propanol, ClCH2CH(OH)CH3, by an S_N2 backside attack on the less hindered primary carbon.

prompt: Which list ranks these compounds from most to least reactive toward S_N2 reaction: CH3Br, CH3OTos, (CH3)3CCl, (CH3)2CHCl?

choices.text: CH3OTos > CH3Br > (CH3)2CHCl > (CH3)3CCl
CH3Br > CH3OTos > (CH3)2CHCl > (CH3)3CCl
choices.why: Tosylate is a better leaving group than bromide, so CH3OTos reacts faster than CH3Br.

choices.text: (CH3)3CCl > (CH3)2CHCl > CH3Br > CH3OTos
choices.why: That's reversed. Methyl substrates with good leaving groups react fastest, and the tertiary chloride slowest.

choices.text: CH3OTos > CH3Br > (CH3)3CCl > (CH3)2CHCl
choices.why: Tertiary substrates don't react by S_N2, so the secondary chloride is more reactive than the tertiary one.

explanation: The two methyl substrates come first, with tosylate the better leaving group: CH3OTos > CH3Br. Then the secondary chloride, which reacts slowly, and last the tertiary chloride, which doesn't react by S_N2 (Exercise 11.3.3).

prompt: How do protic solvents such as methanol and ethanol slow S_N2 reactions?

choices.text: They hydrogen-bond to the nucleophile, caging it and lowering its energy and reactivity
They crowd the substrate's carbon and raise the energy of the transition state
choices.why: Protic solvents act on the nucleophile's ground state, not on the substrate's steric environment.

choices.text: They solvate the metal cation but leave the nucleophilic anion bare
choices.why: That is what polar aprotic solvents do, and it speeds the reaction up.

choices.text: They are too nonpolar to dissolve the salt that supplies the nucleophile
choices.why: Methanol and ethanol are polar. Their effect is to hydrogen-bond to and stabilize the nucleophile.

explanation: Protic solvents (those with an –OH or –NH group) slow S_N2 reactions by solvating the reactant nucleophile. The solvent molecules hydrogen-bond to the nucleophile and form a cage around it, lowering its ground-state energy and therefore its reactivity.

prompt: Which of these solvents is a polar aprotic solvent of the kind that speeds up S_N2 reactions?

choices.text: DMSO, (CH3)2SO
Methanol, CH3OH
choices.why: Methanol has an –OH group, so it's protic, and protic solvents slow S_N2 reactions.

choices.text: Water, H2O
choices.why: Water has –OH groups, so it's protic.

choices.text: Benzene, C6H6
choices.why: Benzene is neither protic nor strongly polar.

explanation: Polar aprotic solvents are polar but have no –OH or –NH group. Acetonitrile (CH3CN), dimethylformamide [(CH3)2NCHO, DMF] and dimethyl sulfoxide [(CH3)2SO, DMSO] are particularly useful; HMPA works too but must be handled with great care.

prompt: Why do polar aprotic solvents such as DMF and DMSO speed up S_N2 reactions?

choices.text: They solvate the metal cations but not the nucleophilic anions, which stay bare and reactive
They hydrogen-bond to the nucleophilic anion and stabilize it in a solvent cage
choices.why: That's what protic solvents do, and it slows the reaction. Aprotic solvents have no –OH or –NH to hydrogen-bond with.

choices.text: They lower the ground-state energy of the nucleophile, making it more reactive
choices.why: They raise it. Lowering the nucleophile's energy would increase ΔG‡ and slow the reaction.

choices.text: They are too nonpolar to dissolve salts, so the nucleophile stays free
choices.why: They are highly polar and dissolve many salts; they just solvate the cations rather than the anions.

explanation: Polar aprotic solvents dissolve many salts because of their high polarity, but they tend to solvate metal cations rather than nucleophilic anions. The bare, unsolvated anions have a higher ground-state energy and greater nucleophilicity, so ΔG‡ decreases and the reaction speeds up.

prompt: For the S_N2 reaction of azide ion with 1-bromobutane, by what factor has the rate been observed to increase on changing the solvent from methanol to HMPA?
explanation: A rate increase of 200,000 has been observed on changing from methanol (protic) to HMPA (polar aprotic). In the section's solvent order, methanol is the slowest and HMPA the fastest, with water, DMSO, DMF and acetonitrile in between.

prompt: Benzene, ether and chloroform are neither protic nor strongly polar. What effect would you expect them to have on the reactivity of a nucleophile in S_N2 reactions?

choices.text: An effect similar to that of protic solvents
An effect similar to that of polar aprotic solvents
choices.why: Polar aprotic solvents work because their high polarity lets them dissolve salts and solvate the cations. These solvents aren't strongly polar.

choices.text: A rate increase even larger than the one HMPA gives
choices.why: HMPA gives the largest increase in the section's solvent list. A weakly polar solvent offers no such advantage.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding to the nucleophile even stronger than in methanol
choices.why: None of these solvents has an –OH or –NH group, so they can't hydrogen-bond to the nucleophile the way protic solvents do.

explanation: Exercise 11.3.4's answer: benzene, ether and chloroform have an effect similar to that of protic solvents. They lack the high polarity that lets polar aprotic solvents dissolve salts and leave the nucleophilic anion bare and reactive.

prompt: According to the section's summary, which two S_N2 variables have their effects felt mainly in the reactant ground state rather than in the transition state?

choices.text: The nucleophile and the solvent
The substrate and the leaving group
choices.why: Those two act mainly on the transition state: hindrance raises it and good leaving groups lower it.

choices.text: The substrate and the solvent
choices.why: The substrate's effect (steric hindrance) is felt in the transition state.

choices.text: The leaving group and the nucleophile
choices.why: The leaving group's effect (charge stabilization) is felt in the transition state.

explanation: Substrate and leaving-group effects are felt primarily in the transition state. Nucleophile and solvent effects are felt primarily in the reactant ground state: a negatively charged nucleophile has a higher ground-state energy, a protic solvent lowers the nucleophile's energy, and a polar aprotic solvent raises it.
